decks.title: Climate of India — Part 1: Controls of climate and the monsoon
goals: Explain how latitude, altitude, distance from the sea, winds, the Himalayas, jet streams and El Niño affect India’s climate
Describe the pattern of temperature, rainfall and winds in summer and in winter
Explain the mechanism of the south-west monsoon

slides.heading: One country, many climates
slides.body_md: Part 1 — India has a **tropical monsoon** climate, yet Leh freezes while Chennai sweats, and Mawsynram floods while western Rajasthan stays dry. Several controls explain the differences.

rows: Mild temperatures, very heavy summer rain

visual.alt: Table of four types of place in India and a typical feature of the climate of each

slides.narration: Namaste! India is one country but has many climates. Mountain towns get snow, the desert bakes, the west coast is drenched in summer, and the Tamil Nadu coast gets its rain in early winter. All of India shares a tropical monsoon climate, but several factors make each region different. In this part we look at those factors and at the monsoon itself.

slides.heading: Factors affecting India’s climate (1)
slides.body_md: **Latitude:** the Tropic of Cancer runs through the middle of India; the south lies in the tropical zone (hot all year), the north in the sub-tropical zone (greater seasonal contrast). **Altitude:** temperature falls with height (about 6.5 °C per km), so hill stations such as Shimla and Ooty are cool. **Distance from the sea (continentality):** the sea warms and cools slowly, so coastal places have a **small annual range** (equable climate) while interior places have a **large range** (extreme climate) — Mumbai’s range is small, Delhi’s large.

rows: South warmer in winter than the north
Shimla cooler than Chandigarh in summer

visual.alt: Table of three climatic factors and examples of their effects

slides.narration: Three factors come first. Latitude: the Tropic of Cancer crosses the middle of India, so the south is hot all year while the north has warm summers and cool winters. Altitude: temperature drops with height, so hill stations are cool. Distance from the sea: the sea heats and cools slowly, so coastal Mumbai has a small difference between summer and winter, while inland Delhi has a large one.

slides.heading: Factors affecting India’s climate (2)
slides.body_md: **Winds:** the seasonal reversal of winds (monsoon) brings rain in summer and dry weather in winter. **The Himalayas:** they block the cold Central Asian winds in winter, keeping north India warmer, and force the monsoon winds to rise and shed rain over the plains. **Jet streams:** fast upper-air westerly winds south of the Himalayas in winter bring **western disturbances**; their shift north in summer, and an easterly jet over the peninsula, help the monsoon set in. **El Niño:** warming of the eastern Pacific Ocean every few years tends to **weaken the Indian monsoon**, causing droughts.

rows: Block cold winds; cause relief rain

visual.alt: Table of four more climatic factors and their effects on India

slides.narration: The monsoon winds themselves change direction with the seasons, bringing rain in summer and dry weather in winter. The Himalayas shut out freezing winds from Central Asia and make the moist monsoon winds rise and rain over the plains. Fast winds high in the sky, called jet streams, guide winter storms into the north and help start the monsoon. And El Niño, a warming of the far Pacific Ocean, often weakens the monsoon.

slides.heading: Summer and winter patterns
slides.body_md: **Summer (March–May):** the sun is overhead near the Tropic of Cancer; temperatures rise from south to north, reaching 45 °C or more in the north-west; a low-pressure area forms over north-west India; hot dry winds (loo) blow in the north. **Winter (December–February):** temperatures fall from south to north; the north-west gets very cold, with frost and snow in the hills; high pressure over the north-west sends dry winds out towards the sea; rain only in the north-west (western disturbances) and on the Tamil Nadu coast.

visual.alt: Table comparing temperature, pressure, winds and rain in summer and winter

slides.narration: In summer the sun shines almost straight down on northern India, so temperatures climb towards the north-west, sometimes above forty five degrees, and a region of low pressure forms there. In winter the pattern reverses: the north-west becomes the coldest part, high pressure builds over it, and dry winds blow out towards the sea. Winter rain falls only in the north-west and on the Tamil Nadu coast.

slides.heading: The monsoon: a seasonal reversal of winds
slides.body_md: The word **monsoon** comes from the Arabic *mausim*, “season”. **Mechanism:** in summer the land heats much faster than the sea; intense **low pressure** develops over north-west India while **high pressure** lies over the Indian Ocean. The **ITCZ** (low-pressure belt) shifts north over the Ganga plain, and the south-east trade winds of the southern hemisphere cross the Equator, are **deflected to the right** (Coriolis effect) and blow as the **south-west monsoon**, laden with moisture. In winter the pressure pattern reverses and dry north-east winds blow from land to sea.

slides.narration: Monsoon means a seasonal wind. In summer the land heats up much faster than the sea, so low pressure develops over north-west India while the ocean stays under high pressure. The trade winds of the southern hemisphere cross the Equator, swing to the right, and blow in from the south-west, full of moisture: the south-west monsoon. In winter the land cools, high pressure forms over it, and dry winds blow out to sea.

slides.heading: Worked example: explaining monsoon behaviour
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** Explain (a) why the south-west monsoon is a moist wind, (b) why it is called “south-west” although it starts as a south-east trade wind, and (c) why the monsoon failed in some El Niño years.

**(a)** It crosses thousands of kilometres of warm Indian Ocean, picking up water vapour.

**(b)** On crossing the Equator, the Earth’s rotation deflects it to the right, so it arrives from the south-west.

**(c)** El Niño warms the eastern Pacific, shifting low pressure away from the Indian region and weakening the pressure difference that drives the monsoon.

visual.alt: Flow of south-east trade winds crossing the Equator and turning into the south-west monsoon

slides.narration: The monsoon is moist because it blows over a huge stretch of warm ocean before reaching India. It begins as a south-east trade wind south of the Equator, but once it crosses the Equator the spin of the Earth turns it to the right, so it arrives from the south-west. In El Niño years the eastern Pacific is unusually warm, which weakens the pressure pattern that pulls the monsoon in, and rainfall can fail.

slides.heading: Arabian Sea and Bay of Bengal branches
slides.body_md: The south-west monsoon reaches the **Kerala coast around 1 June** (the “burst” of the monsoon) and splits into two branches. The **Arabian Sea branch** strikes the Western Ghats, giving very heavy rain on the windward western slopes and little on the leeward Deccan plateau (**rain-shadow area**). The **Bay of Bengal branch** moves north-east, is deflected west by the Himalayas and the Garo–Khasi hills, gives very heavy rain in the north-east (Mawsynram, Cherrapunji) and decreasing rain westward along the Ganga plain. The monsoon covers the whole country by mid-July.

visual.alt: Table of the two branches of the south-west monsoon and the areas they affect

slides.narration: The monsoon arrives on the Kerala coast around the first of June, with a sudden burst of rain, and divides into two branches. The Arabian Sea branch hits the Western Ghats and pours rain on their western slopes, leaving the land beyond in a rain shadow. The Bay of Bengal branch is turned westward by the mountains of the north-east, drenching Meghalaya, and gives less and less rain as it moves up the Ganga plain.

slides.heading: Worked example: why the west coast is wetter
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** Mangaluru on the west coast receives far more rain in July than Bengaluru on the plateau, though both lie at similar latitudes. Explain.

**Step 1.** The Arabian Sea branch meets the Western Ghats almost at right angles.

**Step 2.** Forced to rise, the air cools and its vapour condenses: heavy **orographic (relief) rain** on the windward side, where Mangaluru lies.

**Step 3.** Descending on the leeward side, the air warms and dries, so Bengaluru lies in a partial **rain-shadow**.

nodes.label: Cools, heavy rain on windward side

visual.alt: Flow of relief rainfall over the Western Ghats with a rain-shadow beyond

slides.narration: Both towns lie at about the same latitude, so the difference comes from relief. The monsoon wind blows straight into the Western Ghats, rises, cools and drops heavy rain on the western side, where Mangaluru is. On the far side the air sinks and warms, so it holds on to its moisture, leaving the plateau around Bengaluru much drier.

slides.heading: Summary: Part 1
bullets: Controls: latitude, altitude, distance from the sea, winds, Himalayas, jet streams, El Niño.
Summer: low pressure over the north-west, loo, highest temperatures in the north-west; winter: high pressure, cold north-west, offshore winds.
Monsoon: seasonal reversal of winds caused by differential heating of land and sea and the northward shift of the ITCZ.
Arabian Sea branch: Western Ghats, rain-shadow Deccan; Bay of Bengal branch: north-east India, decreasing westward.

visual.alt: Summary table of pressure and winds in summer and winter

slides.narration: Let us sum up Part 1. India’s climate is controlled by latitude, altitude, distance from the sea, the winds, the Himalayas, jet streams and El Niño. In summer, low pressure over the land draws in the moist south-west monsoon; in winter, high pressure sends dry winds out to sea. The monsoon’s two branches drench the west coast and the north-east.

decks.title: Climate of India — Part 2: Seasons, local winds and climate data
goals: Describe temperature, pressure, winds and rainfall in each of the four seasons
Explain why the Tamil Nadu coast gets rain in winter
Name the local winds and storms of the hot season and explain western disturbances
Calculate annual range and total rainfall from a station’s data and identify its location

slides.heading: The year in four seasons
slides.body_md: Part 2 — the Indian Meteorological Department recognises four seasons. Each has its own pressure, winds and weather, and each leaves a signature in a station’s climate graph.

visual.alt: Table of the four seasons of India and their approximate months

slides.narration: India’s year is divided into four seasons: the hot weather season from March to May, the south-west monsoon from June to September, the retreating monsoon in October and November, and the cold weather season from December to February. Each season has its own winds and weather, and in this part we also learn to read the story of a place’s climate from a graph.

slides.heading: Hot weather and south-west monsoon seasons
slides.body_md: **Hot weather (March–May):** temperatures rise northward; low pressure over the north-west; dry hot winds; local storms (next slide). **South-west monsoon (June–September):** onset in Kerala about 1 June; most of India gets **75–90% of its annual rain**; rainfall is **uncertain and uneven** — with **breaks** of dry spells, heavy rain on windward slopes, and decreasing rain from east to west in the north. Temperatures drop slightly when the rains arrive, but humidity is high.

visual.alt: Table comparing the hot weather and south-west monsoon seasons

slides.narration: In the hot weather season the land heats up steadily and the low pressure over the north-west deepens. Then, from early June, the south-west monsoon arrives and brings most of the year’s rain to most of India. Monsoon rain is uncertain: it may come early or late, and there are dry breaks between wet spells. Temperatures fall a little, but the air stays humid.

slides.heading: Retreating monsoon and cold weather seasons
slides.body_md: **Retreating monsoon (October–November):** the sun moves south, the low pressure over the north weakens and the monsoon withdraws; clear skies and high humidity cause oppressive “**October heat**”. Winds over the Bay of Bengal now blow from the **north-east**, pick up moisture over the bay and bring **heavy rain to the Tamil Nadu coast** (which lies in the rain-shadow of the south-west monsoon). Tropical **cyclones** from the Bay strike the east coast. **Cold weather (December–February):** clear, cool, dry; frost in the north-west; snow in the Himalayas; rain from western disturbances in Punjab and Haryana (useful for wheat).

rows: Cool to cold; frost in NW
NE over the Bay of Bengal
Tamil Nadu coast; cyclones on east coast
Western disturbances in NW; Tamil Nadu

visual.alt: Table comparing the retreating monsoon and cold weather seasons

slides.narration: In October and November the monsoon withdraws as the sun moves south. Skies clear, but humidity stays high, giving uncomfortable October heat. Winds now blow from the north-east across the Bay of Bengal, gather moisture, and bring heavy rain to the Tamil Nadu coast, which missed most of the summer monsoon. Cyclones may strike the east coast. The cold season that follows is clear and dry, with frost in the north-west and snow in the hills.

slides.heading: Local winds and seasonal weather
slides.body_md: **Loo:** strong, hot, dry winds blowing in the afternoons over the northern plains in May–June; can cause heatstroke. **Mango showers:** pre-monsoon thundershowers in Kerala and coastal Karnataka that help mangoes ripen. **Kalbaisakhi** (“calamity of Baisakh”): violent evening thunderstorms with strong winds in West Bengal and Assam in April–May; useful for tea, jute and rice. **Blossom showers:** pre-monsoon showers in Karnataka that help coffee flowers bloom. **Western disturbances:** low-pressure systems from the Mediterranean region, carried east by the westerly jet stream in winter; they bring light rain to Punjab, Haryana and western Uttar Pradesh (good for wheat) and snow to the western Himalayas.

visual.alt: Table of local winds and seasonal weather with season, region and effect

slides.narration: Several local winds and showers have names. The loo is a scorching afternoon wind over the northern plains in early summer. Mango showers in Kerala help mangoes ripen, and blossom showers in Karnataka help coffee plants flower. Kalbaisakhi are violent evening storms in Bengal and Assam that help tea and jute. In winter, western disturbances drift in from the Mediterranean region and bring gentle rain for wheat in the north-west.

slides.heading: Worked example: why does Chennai get winter rain?
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** Chennai receives most of its rain in October–December, unlike most of India. Explain.

**Step 1.** During June–September Chennai lies in the **rain-shadow** of the Western Ghats and the south-west monsoon blows parallel to the coast — little rain.

**Step 2.** In October–November, as the monsoon retreats, winds over the Bay of Bengal blow from the **north-east**.

**Step 3.** Crossing the bay, they pick up moisture and strike the Coromandel coast, giving heavy rain; cyclones add more.

nodes.label: NE winds over Bay of Bengal
Heavy rain on Tamil Nadu coast

visual.alt: Flow explaining the winter rain of the Tamil Nadu coast

slides.narration: During the summer monsoon, Chennai is sheltered by the Western Ghats and the winds blow along its coast rather than onto it, so it gets little rain. When the monsoon retreats, winds over the Bay of Bengal swing round to come from the north-east. They gather moisture over the bay and hit the Tamil Nadu coast head-on, giving it most of its rain in October to December.

notes.title: Climate of India — Notes

sections.heading: 1. Factors affecting India’s climate
sections.body_md:
- **Latitude:** Tropic of Cancer divides India into a tropical south and sub-tropical north.
- **Altitude:** temperature falls with height (hill stations cool).
- **Distance from the sea:** coastal places equable (small range, e.g. Mumbai), interior places extreme (large range, e.g. Delhi).
- **Monsoon winds:** seasonal reversal → wet summers, dry winters.
- **Himalayas:** block cold Central Asian winds; make monsoon winds rise and rain over the plains.
- **Jet streams:** westerly jet in winter steers western disturbances; changes in the jets help the monsoon set in.
- **El Niño:** warm eastern Pacific → often a weak monsoon and drought in India.

key_terms.definition_md: A climate with a small difference between summer and winter temperatures, typical of coastal places.
An occasional warming of the eastern Pacific Ocean that tends to weaken the Indian monsoon.

visual.alt: Table of three factors and their effects

sections.heading: 2. Summer and winter patterns
sections.body_md:
| Feature | Summer (Mar–May) | Winter (Dec–Feb) |
|---|---|---|
| Temperature | Rises northward; highest in NW | Falls northward; coldest in NW |
| Pressure over NW India | Low | High |
| Winds | Hot dry winds (loo); onshore later | Dry offshore NE winds |
| Rain | Pre-monsoon showers | Western disturbances (NW); Tamil Nadu coast |

key_terms.definition_md: A hot, dry, strong afternoon wind of the northern plains in May and June.

visual.alt: Table of extreme areas in each season

sections.heading: 3. The monsoon and its mechanism
sections.body_md:
- **Monsoon:** seasonal reversal of winds (Arabic *mausim*, season).
- **Mechanism:** differential heating in summer → low pressure over NW India, high pressure over the Indian Ocean; ITCZ shifts north; SE trades cross the Equator, are deflected right (Coriolis) → moist **SW monsoon**.
- **Onset:** Kerala about 1 June (“burst”); covers India by mid-July.
- **Arabian Sea branch:** heavy rain on windward Western Ghats; rain-shadow on the leeward Deccan.
- **Bay of Bengal branch:** heavy rain in the north-east (Meghalaya); deflected west along the Ganga plain, rain decreasing westward.
- **Winter:** pressure reverses; dry NE monsoon from land to sea.

key_terms.definition_md: An area on the leeward side of mountains that receives little rain.
The sudden onset of heavy monsoon rain, usually on the Kerala coast around 1 June.

visual.alt: Table of monsoon branches

sections.heading: 4. The four seasons
sections.body_md:
1. **Hot weather (Mar–May):** rising temperatures, low pressure in NW, local storms.
2. **SW monsoon (Jun–Sep):** 75–90% of annual rain; uncertain, uneven, with breaks.
3. **Retreating monsoon (Oct–Nov):** withdrawal; “October heat”; NE winds over the Bay bring heavy rain to the Tamil Nadu coast; cyclones on the east coast.
4. **Cold weather (Dec–Feb):** clear, cool, dry; frost in NW; snow in the Himalayas; western disturbances.

The Tamil Nadu coast lies in the rain-shadow of the SW monsoon and gets most rain from the retreating/NE monsoon.

key_terms.definition_md: The withdrawal of the south-west monsoon in October and November, when north-east winds over the Bay of Bengal bring rain to the Tamil Nadu coast.

visual.alt: Table of the four seasons

sections.heading: 5. Local winds and seasonal weather
sections.body_md:
| Name | When | Where | Effect |
|---|---|---|---|
| Loo | May–June | Northern plains | Hot, dry; heatstroke |
| Mango showers | Apr–May | Kerala, coastal Karnataka | Ripening of mangoes |
| Blossom showers | Apr–May | Karnataka | Coffee flowering |
| Kalbaisakhi | Apr–May | West Bengal, Assam | Violent storms; helps tea, jute, rice |
| Western disturbances | Winter | NW India | Rain for wheat; Himalayan snow |

key_terms.definition_md: Low-pressure systems from the Mediterranean region that bring winter rain to north-west India.
Violent evening thunderstorms of West Bengal and Assam in April and May.

visual.alt: Table of two local weather types and regions

sections.heading: 6. Interpreting climate data
sections.body_md:
- **Annual range** = highest monthly mean temperature − lowest monthly mean temperature.
- **Total rainfall** = sum of the 12 monthly totals.
- Small range (under about 8 °C) → coastal or southern; large range (over about 15 °C) → interior, northern.
- Rain peak Jun–Sep → SW monsoon region; peak Oct–Dec → Tamil Nadu coast; some Jan–Feb rain → NW India (western disturbances).
- Very heavy Jun–Sep rain with a small range → west coast or north-east hills.

key_terms.definition_md: The difference between the mean temperatures of the hottest and coldest months.

notes.exam_tips_md:
**Common mistakes**
- Saying winds blow from low to high pressure.
- Placing the rain-shadow on the windward side.
- Attributing Tamil Nadu’s winter rain to the south-west monsoon.
- Computing annual range from rainfall figures.

**How marks are usually awarded**

questions.stem_md: Give two ways in which the Himalayas influence the climate of India.

answer.model_answer_md: They act as a barrier to the bitterly cold winds from Central Asia, keeping north India warmer in winter; they force the moist monsoon winds to rise, giving heavy rain to the northern plains and north-east (and trap the monsoon within the subcontinent).

questions.solution_md: Barrier; relief rain.

questions.stem_md: Explain how (a) distance from the sea, (b) altitude and (c) the jet stream affect the climate of named parts of India.

answer.model_answer_md: (a) Coastal Mumbai or Chennai has a small annual range because the sea heats and cools slowly; interior Delhi or Nagpur has a large range. (b) Hill stations such as Shimla, Darjeeling or Ooty are cool because temperature falls with height. (c) The westerly jet stream steers western disturbances into Punjab, Haryana and Jammu and Kashmir in winter, bringing rain and snow; its shift northward in summer helps the monsoon to set in.

questions.solution_md: Continentality; altitude; jet stream.

questions.stem_md: Explain the mechanism of the south-west monsoon in three steps.

answer.model_answer_md: (1) In summer the land heats much faster than the sea, creating intense low pressure over north-west India while high pressure lies over the Indian Ocean. (2) The ITCZ shifts north over the Ganga plain, and the south-east trade winds are drawn across the Equator towards this low. (3) On crossing the Equator they are deflected to the right by the Earth’s rotation and blow from the south-west, laden with moisture from the ocean.

questions.solution_md: Heating → pressure → deflected moist winds.

questions.stem_md:
(a) Name two factors that make the climate of Mumbai different from that of Delhi. [2]

(b) How does El Niño affect the Indian monsoon? [2]

(c) Explain the role of the Himalayas in the climate of India. [3]

(d) Explain how the jet stream and western disturbances affect the weather of north-west India in winter. [3]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) Distance from the sea (Mumbai coastal, equable; Delhi interior, extreme) and latitude (Delhi farther north, colder winters); also rainfall from the Arabian Sea branch.

(b) El Niño, a warming of the eastern Pacific, weakens the pressure contrast that drives the monsoon, so India often gets deficient rain or drought.

(c) They block cold Central Asian winds, keeping north India warmer in winter; they force the monsoon winds to rise, causing heavy rain on the plains and the north-east; they confine the monsoon to the subcontinent.

(d) The westerly jet stream, flowing south of the Himalayas in winter, carries western disturbances from the Mediterranean region into north-west India; these bring cloudy weather, light rain for the wheat crop and snow in the western Himalayas.

questions.solution_md: Factors; El Niño; Himalayas; jet stream.

questions.stem_md:
(a) What is meant by the monsoon? [2]

(b) State two features of monsoon rainfall in India. [2]

(c) Explain the mechanism by which the south-west monsoon is set up over India. [3]

(d) Explain why (i) the western slopes of the Western Ghats receive heavy rain, (ii) Meghalaya receives very heavy rain and (iii) rainfall decreases westward along the Ganga plain. [3]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) A seasonal reversal of winds: moist south-west winds from sea to land in summer and dry north-east winds from land to sea in winter.

(b) Uncertain (onset and amount vary); uneven in distribution; with breaks; most rain in four months (any two).

(c) The land heats more than the sea, creating low pressure over north-west India and high pressure over the Indian Ocean; the ITCZ moves north; south-east trades cross the Equator, are deflected right and blow as moist south-west winds.

(d) (i) The Arabian Sea branch strikes the Ghats at right angles and rises — relief rain. (ii) The Bay of Bengal branch is funnelled into the Khasi hills and forced up. (iii) The winds lose moisture as they move inland.

questions.solution_md: Definition; features; mechanism; three reasons.

questions.stem_md:
(a) Name the four seasons of India with their months. [2]

(b) What is “October heat”? Why does it occur? [2]

(c) Explain why the Coromandel coast gets heavy rain in winter while most of India is dry. [3]

(d) Name and describe three local weather phenomena of the hot weather season. [3]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) Hot weather (March–May), south-west monsoon (June–September), retreating monsoon (October–November), cold weather (December–February).

(b) Hot and humid weather in October; the monsoon has withdrawn and skies clear, but the ground and air are still moist, so the heat is oppressive.

(c) As the monsoon retreats, winds over the Bay of Bengal blow from the north-east; they pick up moisture and strike the Tamil Nadu coast; cyclones add more rain. In summer this coast is in the rain-shadow.

(d) Loo — hot dry afternoon wind of the northern plains; mango showers — pre-monsoon rain in Kerala and coastal Karnataka that ripens mangoes; Kalbaisakhi — violent evening storms of Bengal and Assam that help tea and jute (also blossom showers in Karnataka).

questions.solution_md: Seasons; October heat; Coromandel rain; local weather.

(b) 736 mm.

(c) July–August (south-west monsoon season), brought by the Bay of Bengal branch of the south-west monsoon; interior, because the annual range (19.5 °C) is large (extreme climate).

Station P has temperatures (°C) 24.4, 24.9, 26.9, 28.6, 30, 29, 27.5, 27.2, 27.5, 28.6, 27.6, 25.9 and rainfall (mm) 1, 1, 0, 1, 12, 520, 690, 430, 320, 70, 15, 3. Station R has temperatures 24.5, 25.5, 27.5, 30.5, 32.5, 32.5, 31, 30.5, 30, 28, 26, 25 and rainfall 25, 8, 6, 15, 45, 50, 90, 115, 120, 280, 350, 140.

answer.model_answer_md:
